settings.heading:
Bodology for Mood:
The Studies
settings.subtext: Mood and metabolism are wired together. Unstable blood sugar means unstable energy supply to the brain — and inositol itself is a second messenger in serotonin signalling. The mood evidence for inositol is earlier-stage than the metabolic evidence. Here's what exists, reported straight.*

settings.label: Placebo-controlled
settings.popup_text: A "placebo-controlled" study is one in which one group receives the actual compound while another receives an inactive look-alike, or placebo. This lets researchers separate the compound's physical effects from the effect of believing it works.

settings.label: Double-blind
settings.popup_text: "Double-blind" means neither participants nor researchers know who receives which product, preventing bias and ensuring objective results.

settings.label: Am J Psychiatry
settings.popup_text: This trial was published in the American Journal of Psychiatry — one of the field's most established journals. The authors themselves called for replication, and we'd rather show you that honesty than hide it.

settings.title: Study 1 Overview
settings.background_text: An independent double-blind, placebo-controlled trial: 12 g of inositol daily (n = 13) versus placebo (n = 15) for 4 weeks, in patients with low mood. The rationale: spinal-fluid inositol had been reported lower than normal in this group (Levine et al., 1995).†

settings.label: What is the Hamilton scale
settings.popup_text: The Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HDRS) is the standard clinician-rated scale used in research to score low-mood symptoms. In this trial, overall improvement on the scale was significantly greater with inositol than placebo at week 4.

settings.label: A note on the dose
settings.popup_text: Mood research has used 12 g of inositol per day — three times a standard Bodology serving (4 g). We show the study as it was run. The 4 g dose is the one studied for metabolic outcomes.

settings.text:
†Study 1: Levine J, Barak Y, Gonzalves M, Szor H, Elizur A, Kofman O, Belmaker RH. Double-blind, controlled trial of inositol treatment of depression. Am J Psychiatry. 1995;152(5):792–794. DOI: 10.1176/ajp.152.5.792. Small trial; the authors called replication "crucial." Study population was patients in psychiatric care — this is independent research on inositol, not on Bodology, and not a claim about treating any condition.

settings.label: Meta-analysis
settings.popup_text: A meta-analysis pools the results of many independent trials into a single estimate — the strongest form of evidence for an overall effect. This one pooled every double-blind randomized inositol mood trial to 2013.

settings.label: Mixed results
settings.popup_text: Pooled across all trials, inositol's effect on mood did not reach statistical significance. It showed marginally more responders than placebo (p = 0.06), with the strongest signal in premenstrual mood symptoms (p = 0.07). Early and promising in specific groups — not yet proven overall.

settings.title: Study 2 Overview — the meta-analysis
settings.background_text: A meta-analysis pooling the double-blind randomized trials of inositol for mood and anxiety to 2013: seven mood trials (n = 242) and four anxiety trials (n = 70). Pooled results did not reach statistical significance overall; inositol showed marginally more responders than placebo (p = 0.06), with the strongest signal in premenstrual mood symptoms (p = 0.07). Translation: early and promising in specific groups, not yet proven overall. We'd rather tell you that than oversell it (Mukai et al., 2014).‡

settings.text:
‡Study 2: Mukai T, Kishi T, Matsuda Y, Iwata N. A meta-analysis of inositol for depression and anxiety disorders. Hum Psychopharmacol. 2014;29(1):55–63. DOI: 10.1002/hup.2369. Trial doses in the pooled studies were higher than a standard Bodology serving. All studies cited are independent research on inositol, not on Bodology.
